en.title: Michael Mann's Underrated 'B-Sides' Shine in New Podcast Deep Dive
en.summary: Discover the often-overlooked films of cinematic master Michael Mann, explored in a fascinating new episode of The B-Side podcast. Dive into the troubled production of 'The Keep' and the enduring legacy of his digital aesthetic.
en.body:
Michael Mann is a filmmaker whose name conjures images of neon-drenched cityscapes, meticulously crafted heists, and intense, stoic protagonists. While films like **Heat** and **The Last of the Mohicans** have cemented his legendary status, a recent episode of **The B-Side** podcast, featuring **Blake Howard** of One Heat Minute Productions, turns its attention to the director's "B-sides" – the films made in between his more famous works.

This deep dive explores movies like the atmospheric horror **The Keep**, the ambitious but troubled crime drama **Public Enemies**, the divisive sci-fi thriller **Blackhat**, and the much-anticipated **Ferrari**. The conversation delves into the unique challenges and triumphs of Mann's filmmaking process, highlighting his unwavering commitment to his vision. The troubled making of **The Keep**, for instance, is discussed alongside its iconic Tangerine Dream score, a collaboration that has become as legendary as the film's production woes. The episode also touches upon Mann's fascination with historical narratives, noting the surprising scarcity of films about the French-Indian War, a period he explored in **The Last of the Mohicans**.

## The Enduring Allure of Mann's 'In-Between' Films

What makes Mann's "B-sides" so compelling, and why do they often achieve greater acclaim retrospectively than upon their initial release? The podcast explores how Mann's films, even those that underperformed at the box office, possess a distinctive quality that resonates with audiences over time. His pioneering work with digital cinematography, an evolving aesthetic that pushed the boundaries of filmmaking, is a recurring theme. The episode also addresses the intense, demanding nature of working with Mann, referencing a quote from producer Amy Pascal who likened the experience to childbirth: "You forget about the pain of childbirth too. I mean, whatever you go through, you still want another baby. It's like that with Michael too." This speaks volumes about the director's exacting standards and the unforgettable experiences he crafts on set.

## A Legacy of Visionary Cinema

The discussion provides valuable context for fans who appreciate Mann's unique directorial voice. It underscores how even his less commercially successful films contribute significantly to his overall artistic legacy, showcasing a consistent pursuit of cinematic excellence and innovation. The podcast's exploration of **Public Enemies**, for example, touches on the contentious star-director relationship during its production, a testament to Mann's uncompromising approach. For cinephiles and casual viewers alike, these "B-sides" offer a richer understanding of a filmmaker who consistently challenges himself and his audience, leaving an indelible mark on cinema.

## What's Next

While no new Michael Mann projects are immediately on the horizon, the conversation around his filmography continues to evolve. Fans can revisit **Ferrari**, his most recent directorial effort, and delve into the extensive back catalog discussed on **The B-Side** podcast, available through their preferred listening platforms.

content_raw: Welcome to The B-Side! Here we talk about movie directors! Not the movies that made them famous or kept them famous, but the ones that they made in between.  Today we discuss the great Michael Mann! Our B-Sides are The Keep , Public Enemies , Blackhat , and Ferrari . Our guest is the iconic Blake Howard of One Heat Minute Productions .  We talk the troubled making of The Keep , as well as that incredible Tangerine Dream score. The legendary Twilight Zone episode “The Howling Man” also comes up. There’s also mention of how many movies about the French-Indian War there are (spoiler alert: not many ).  Blake, Conor, and I discuss the legacy of Mann and his recent output of underappreciated films. Why is it that Michael Mann’s films are often released to lesser success than their long-term reputations suggest? There’s celebration of Mann’s ever-evolving digital aesthetic, conversation about the contentious star-director relationship on the set of Public Enemies , and his demanding, exacting instincts. As legendary producer Amy Pascal once put it about working with the director: “You forget about the pain of childbirth too. I mean, whatever you go through, you still want another baby. It’s like that with Michael too.” Listen below and subscribe here . Be sure to give us a follow on Bluesky at @tfsbside.bsky.social . Enjoy!
